<explanation>
Based on our analysis of the file tree and README, pdfcpu is a Go-based PDF processing library that offers both an API and a comprehensive CLI for handling and manipulating PDFs. It is a full-fledged PDF processor that can perform functions such as encryption, splitting, merging, stamping, form handling, and more. In addition to its core processing functionalities, pdfcpu also includes tests, sample PDFs, and scripts to illustrate and validate its features.

Below are guidelines on how to create a detailed system design diagram for pdfcpu:

1. Identify the Main Components:
   - User Interface / CLI: Represented by the command-line interface in the “cmd/pdfcpu” directory and the related CLI code under “pkg/cli”. This is the entry point for users who invoke pdfcpu operations.
   - API Layer: Found in “pkg/api”. It exposes functionalities for PDF processing that can be consumed either directly in Go projects or indirectly via the CLI.
   - Core Processing Engine: Centered around “pkg/pdfcpu” and its subdirectories (like “pkg/pdfcpu/model”, “pkg/pdfcpu/primitives”, “pkg/pdfcpu/write”, “pkg/pdfcpu/read”, etc.). This is where the heart of PDF processing logic resides (e.g., parsing, validation, drawing, PDF manipulation).
   - Supporting Modules:
       • Filter Component (“pkg/filter”): Implements PDF-specific filters and decoding routines.
       • Font Handling (“pkg/font” and “internal/corefont”): Manages both core fonts and user fonts, including metrics and installation routines.
       • Logging (“pkg/log”): For logging operations during various processing stages.
   - External Interfaces & Scripts: The “_scripts” directory holds bash scripts for batch operations (like encryption, extraction, merging, etc.) and can be shown as utilities that drive the core library.
   - Test & Sample Components: While not the focus of the production architecture, the “pkg/samples” and “pkg/api/test” directories demonstrate how the engine is used.
   - Configuration & CI/CD: Directories like “.github”, “.goreleaser.yml”, and “Dockerfile” illustrate how the project is built, tested, and deployed.

2. Determine Relationships and Interactions:
   - The CLI (from “cmd/pdfcpu” and “pkg/cli”) takes commands from the user and translates them into calls to the API layer (“pkg/api”).
   - The API layer acts as a façade over the core processing engine (“pkg/pdfcpu”), orchestrating operations such as merging, stamping, or resizing PDFs.
   - The core processing engine calls lower-level utilities (filtering, font handling, logging, etc.) and manipulates PDF structures using models defined in “pkg/pdfcpu/model” and similar subdirectories.
   - Internal support for PDF features is modularized into sub-packages (e.g., for encryption, form handling, annotations) which interact with both the API layer and the CLI.
   - The scripts and CI/CD configuration automate tests and package releases, indirectly ensuring the stability of interactions among components.

3. Highlight Key Architectural Patterns and Design Principles:
   - Layered Architecture: The separation between the CLI, API, core engine, and supporting libraries demonstrates a clear layered design.
   - Modularity: Distinct packages (like “pkg/filter”, “pkg/font”, “pkg/api”, etc.) show a modular approach, where each module is responsible for a specific set of tasks.
   - Separation of Concerns: For example, the CLI deals solely with user input and command parsing, while the core engine takes responsibility for PDF processing.
   - Testability: The presence of extensive tests in “pkg/api/test” and “pkg/cli/test” underscores an emphasis on reliability through unit and integration testing.

4. Include Relevant Technologies:
   - The project is written in Go.
   - It uses standard Go modules (visible in the “go.mod” file).
   - CI/CD is configured through GitHub Actions workflows.
   - Docker is used for containerized builds and running pdfcpu.

5. Guidelines for Tailoring the Diagram:
   - For this full-stack PDF processing library, ensure the diagram clearly separates the CLI from the API and further delineates the processing engine from utility/support components.
   - Group similar components together (for example, combine all font and metrics functionality in one cluster, all filtering functionality in another).
   - Use directional arrows to show that the CLI calls into the API, the API interacts with the core engine, and the core engine utilizes supporting modules.
   - Optionally add external elements (like sample PDFs or test harnesses) to show how client applications or users might interact with pdfcpu.

6. Elements to Include in Your Diagram:
   - Labels: Each component should be clearly labeled – for instance, “CLI Interface (cmd/pdfcpu, pkg/cli)”, “API Layer (pkg/api)”, “Core Processing Engine (pkg/pdfcpu and sub-packages)”, “Filters (pkg/filter)”, “Font & Metrics (pkg/font, internal/corefont)”, “Logging (pkg/log)”, etc.
   - Directional Arrows: Draw arrows from CLI → API, and from API → Core Engine, then branching out into supporting modules.
   - Visual Differentiation: Consider color coding layers (e.g., one color for user interface components, another for core services, another for support libraries). Alternatively, use different shapes (e.g., rectangles for modules, cylinders for databases if any, even though pdfcpu doesn’t involve a database, you could label the scripts and configuration as utilities).

7. Final Tips:
   - Aim for clarity and detail. While you want to capture as many essential elements as possible, don’t overwhelm with every file – focus on logical groupings that represent the system’s architecture.
   - Make sure that the interaction flow (from user/CLI invocation to internal PDF processing) is clearly visible and annotated.
   - If space permits, add a brief note or legend to explain any color coding or shape differences used.

Using these guidelines, your system design diagram will effectively represent how pdfcpu is architected, showing the interaction between the CLI, API, core processing engine, and supporting modules—all while highlighting the modular, layered design that underpins this comprehensive PDF processing tool.
</explanation>
